content:
## Decision

**Primary architecture:** persistent native Rust sidecar helper process. Electron launches it on app start, communicates with it over a length-prefixed JSON-RPC channel on a UNIX domain socket (Linux/macOS) or named pipe (Windows). The sidecar owns capture, encode, rolling segments, and export/remux. Electron remains UI and control plane only.

**Fallback architecture:** ffmpeg-driven helper process with PipeWire input on Linux. Same sidecar shape, same IPC contract, but the inner engine is a managed ffmpeg child process driven by carefully chosen flags (`-f pipewire` input, hardware encoder selection, `-f segment` for rolling buffer, separate concat invocation for export).

**Rejected:**

- Per-command standalone native binary launched on demand (one of the framings of candidate 1) — does not fit a continuously running replay ring buffer.
- Node N-API addon linked into Electron main (candidate 2) — packaging matrix per Electron version, ABI coupling, native crash takes down the UI, hostile to solo maintenance.

## Why the primary won

Capture stability is the single highest-priority axis. The v1.1.0 ceiling (1080p60 stable, 1440p60/4K60 not stable, RTX 4080 Super not the bottleneck) is caused by frames being dropped before any encoder sees them — inside Chromium MediaRecorder + canvas scaling. The only architecture that fully escapes that path is one where:

1. Capture runs in its own native scheduler, not on Electron's main loop.
2. Frame data path is dmabuf or shm directly into the encoder, not through JS or canvas.
3. Crash isolation from Electron's UI process is structural, not best-effort.

A persistent native sidecar gives all three. An N-API addon shares Electron's main process and gives up isolation. An on-demand child binary cannot maintain a continuous rolling buffer. An ffmpeg helper gives most of this but at the cost of driving ffmpeg's CLI as a brittle wrapper.

## Encoder backend strategy

The sidecar exposes a single `EncoderBackend` trait with implementations:

- `NvencEncoder` (NVIDIA Video Codec SDK / NVENC)
- `VaapiEncoder` (libva — covers AMD and Intel on Linux)
- `QsvEncoder` (oneVPL — Intel discrete / Arc on Windows; fallback to VAAPI on Linux)
- `AmfEncoder` (AMD AMF on Windows, later)
- `X264Encoder` (libx264 via libavcodec — CPU fallback)

Probe order: NVENC → VAAPI/QSV → AMF → x264. The implementation can use the `ffmpeg-next` Rust crate to bind libavcodec so the engine gets every hardware encoder ffmpeg supports without shelling out to the ffmpeg CLI. This is the line that separates the primary from the fallback: primary links libav*; fallback execs ffmpeg.

## Capture frontend strategy

`CaptureSource` trait:

- `PipeWireSource` — Linux/Wayland first. Uses xdg-desktop-portal `ScreenCast` interface + `pipewire-rs` for the dmabuf stream.
- `WgcSource` — Windows later. Windows.Graphics.Capture via `windows-rs`. DXGI Desktop Duplication as a fallback.
- macOS is out of scope for v2.0.0 but the trait shape leaves it possible.

## Rolling segment design

Ring buffer of in-memory encoded GOPs (no on-disk write amplification during normal replay-buffer operation). Buffer length is configured by the user (the "last N minutes" replay window). On "save replay" the engine remuxes the live ring buffer to MP4 directly without touching the capture pipeline. Implementation details belong to T-006.

## Instant replay export / remux

The engine performs the remux itself via libavformat (no separate ffmpeg CLI process). This eliminates the v1.1.0 finalization race where the encoder process and the saver process compete. Detailed design belongs to T-007.

## Packaging

`electron-builder` ships the platform-specific sidecar binary as an `extraResources` entry per target. Rust produces a single statically-linked binary per platform (or a binary plus a known set of system shared libs). No node-gyp / electron-rebuild ABI coupling. macOS code signing of the helper is the only nontrivial item and is deferred until the macOS target is on the table.

Every shipped binary, including the helper, must get a `.sha256` sidecar per the project release rule.

## Debuggability

The sidecar is runnable standalone from a terminal with the same IPC server enabled and a simple `cove-replay-engine probe` / `cove-replay-engine capture --to /tmp/out.mp4` set of dev subcommands. Engine logs go to a file under the user data dir; Electron tails the log and can surface engine errors in the UI.

## Failure isolation

If the sidecar crashes, Electron main process detects the IPC channel closing, surfaces the error in the UI, and offers a one-click restart. The UI does not crash with the engine. This is the structural property an N-API addon cannot offer.

## Maintenance burden — solo-maintainer fit

Rust + cargo gives a single-command, reproducible build per platform. No node-gyp / NAPI version churn. The encoder backend abstraction concentrates the complexity in one trait. The ffmpeg fallback path remains available as an escape hatch if any encoder backend implementation slips.

## What this decision does NOT do

- It does not write any Rust code.
- It does not pick the exact IPC framing yet (JSON-RPC vs Cap'n Proto vs bincode — T-008 decides).
- It does not pick the exact rolling buffer data structure (T-006).
- It does not commit to a specific NVENC SDK version (T-005).
- It does not change any source file. Only `.story/` planning state changes.

## Hard constraint reaffirmed

Do not continue patching the v1 MediaRecorder pipeline as the long-term v2 solution. v1.1.0 stays as the stable baseline; v2.0.0 is the architectural shift.
title: v2 replay engine architecture decision (T-003)
